name: Value Investing
oneLiner: Estimating what a business is worth, then paying meaningfully less than that.
thesis:
Value investing treats a share as a fractional claim on a business rather than a ticker that moves. Practitioners in this tradition first estimate what the whole business is plausibly worth — from its assets, its earnings power, or the cash it can be expected to throw off — and then compare that estimate with the price the market is asking. Benjamin Graham's framing was that the market is there to quote prices, not to tell you what things are worth, and that the gap between the two is the only thing an investor is being paid to notice. The gap itself is the **margin of safety**: room for the estimate to be wrong and for the outcome still to be tolerable.

The difficulty is that a low price is not evidence of a mistake by anyone else. A business can be cheap because it is shrinking, because its industry is being displaced, or because its accounting flatters it — the well-documented **value trap**. Estimates of intrinsic value are opinions dressed as arithmetic, and two careful analysts can differ by a factor of two on the same company. Nothing here says the approach works, produces a profit, or fits any particular person; it describes how a school of investors has said they think.
entryRules: Value investors typically start from an estimate of intrinsic value built from the business itself — assets, normalised earnings, or expected free cash flow — before looking at what the share is quoted at.

Graham's students have described requiring a **margin of safety**: a price far enough below their own estimate that an ordinary error in the estimate would not be ruinous. The size of that discount is a judgement call, not a formula.
Many in this tradition have said they only consider businesses they can actually describe — Buffett's **circle of competence** idea — and pass on anything whose economics they cannot explain simply.
Balance-sheet strength is commonly examined before the valuation is trusted, on the reasoning that a heavily indebted business may not survive long enough for any gap to close.
Practitioners frequently distinguish a business that is cheap from one that is merely falling, and have written at length about how hard that distinction is to make in advance.
exitRules: The most commonly stated exit in this school is the price approaching the investor's own estimate of value — the reason for holding was the gap, so the gap closing removes the reason.

Value investors also describe selling when the original thesis is contradicted by the business rather than by the price: margins that were supposed to recover do not, or the moat turns out not to exist.
Some, Buffett prominently, have described holding certain businesses indefinitely and revising the value estimate upward instead of selling — a position that other value investors explicitly reject.
Recognising that an estimate was simply wrong is treated in this literature as its own exit, separate from any price move, and is widely described as the hardest one to act on.
riskManagement: The **value trap** is the signature failure mode: a share that is cheap on today's numbers because the numbers are about to get worse. No screen distinguishes it from a bargain in advance, and investors in this tradition have lost substantial capital to it.
A gap between price and estimated value can persist for years, or never close at all. There is no mechanism guaranteeing that the market ever agrees with an analyst's estimate.

Because the discipline encourages buying what is falling, positions frequently move against the buyer after purchase. Practitioners describe sizing positions so that being early is survivable, and avoiding borrowed money for that reason.
Concentration cuts both ways. Some value investors hold very few positions on the argument that good ideas are rare; that same concentration magnifies the cost of a single mistaken estimate.

The **riskLevel** shown here is a rough comparative signal against the other strategies in this app. It is not a measurement, and it says nothing about whether this approach suits any particular reader.

guideCards.headline: A price is a fact. A value is an opinion.
guideCards.body: One you read off a screen. The other you build from the business: its assets, its earnings, the cash it throws off. Value investing is the claim that the two drift apart, and the gap between them is the whole subject.

guideCards.headline: The gap is error tolerance, not a bargain.
guideCards.body: Your estimate of what a business is worth is a guess with error bars. Two careful analysts can differ by half. Paying well below your own number is what lets the estimate be wrong and the outcome still be survivable. {{book:the-intelligent-investor|Graham}} called it the **margin of safety**.

guideCards.title: A gap that stayed open
guideCards.caption: Eight years, and the quoted price never reached the estimate. Nothing in a market obliges the two lines to meet. Illustration, not data.

guideCards.prompt: Company filings are public. So where is the advantage supposed to come from?

options.label: Holding a position that looks wrong for years

guideCards.explanation: The filings sit on the same website for everyone. What is scarce is the willingness to own something the market is still marking down, and the balance sheet to survive doing it.

guideCards.headline: Most participants are not allowed to wait.
guideCards.body: The claimed edge is structural as much as behavioural. Money managers report quarterly and lose clients after two bad years. A position that needs five years before it can be judged is not one most of them can hold, whatever they believe about it.

guideCards.title: Practising it did not prevent this
guideCards.caption: {{trader:warren-buffett|Buffett}} listed these four falls in Berkshire's own shares in the 2017 Berkshire letter, to argue against owning stocks with borrowed money.

guideCards.body: A share can be cheap because the market is wrong, or cheap because next year's numbers will be worse than this year's. The second one is the [[1]], and no screen separates it from the first in advance.
guideCards.explanation: Cheapness is a symptom, not a diagnosis. The same low multiple appears on a business the market has misjudged and on one that is quietly shrinking.

guideCards.body: Before treating a low price as somebody else's mistake, value investors describe checking the ordinary reasons it might be correct.

guideCards.headline: The edge is not a settled fact.
guideCards.body: In their 2020 paper The Value Premium, Eugene Fama and Kenneth French found US value premiums much lower after 1991 than before. Their own caveat: monthly returns are noisy enough that they could not rule out the expected premium being unchanged.

guideCards.headline: You can only estimate what you understand.
guideCards.body: {{trader:warren-buffett|Buffett}} wrote in the 1996 Berkshire letter that the size of an investor's circle of competence matters far less than knowing where its edge is. That is a limit on the method: no estimate, no gap, nothing to act on.

guideCards.title: What the method asks of you
guideCards.summary: A bet on the gap between price and estimated worth, paid for in years of looking wrong.
bullets: The margin of safety exists so a wrong estimate is still survivable.
The claimed edge is tolerance and time horizon, not private information.
Cheap and mispriced are different things, and no screen tells them apart.
Nothing forces a price to ever agree with an estimate.

guideCards.insight: A gap between price and value is not a promise that it closes. It is a reason to hold an opinion, and time enough to be wrong.
